# 2. Data Loading from HDFS

## Description

The MovieLens 100K dataset is stored in the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS). In this step, the raw dataset is loaded into Apache Spark as Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs).

Three datasets are imported:

- **u.user** – user demographic information
- **u.data** – movie rating records
- **u.item** – movie metadata

The datasets are loaded as RDDs because they provide a flexible low-level abstraction for distributed data processing before being transformed into structured Spark DataFrames in the next stage.

# 3. Convert RDDs into Spark DataFrames

## Description

After loading the raw datasets from HDFS as RDDs, the next step is to convert them into Spark DataFrames.

Compared with RDDs, DataFrames provide a structured representation of the data with predefined schemas, enabling Spark SQL optimisation and more efficient analytical processing.

- **ratingDF** – Movie rating records
- **movieDF** – Movie metadata together with genre indicators

Each DataFrame is assigned an explicit schema to ensure data consistency before further preprocessing and storage.

%spark

// ============================================
// STEP 3.1 Create User DataFrame
// ============================================

println("=" * 60)
println("CREATING USER DATAFRAME")
println("=" * 60)

val userSchema = StructType(Array(
  StructField("user_id", IntegerType, true),
  StructField("age", IntegerType, true),
  StructField("gender", StringType, true),
  StructField("occupation", StringType, true),
  StructField("zip_code", StringType, true)
))

val userRowRDD = userRDD.map { line =>
  val parts = line.split("\\|")
  Row(
    parts(0).toInt,
    parts(1).toInt,
    parts(2),
    parts(3),
    parts(4)
  )
}

val userDF = spark.createDataFrame(userRowRDD, userSchema)

println("\nUser DataFrame Schema")
userDF.printSchema()

println("\nSample User Data")
userDF.show(5, false)


// ============================================
// STEP 3.2 Create Rating DataFrame
// ============================================

println("=" * 60)
println("CREATING RATING DATAFRAME")
println("=" * 60)

val ratingSchema = StructType(Array(
  StructField("user_id", IntegerType, true),
  StructField("movie_id", IntegerType, true),
  StructField("rating", IntegerType, true),
  StructField("timestamp", LongType, true)
))

val ratingRowRDD = ratingRDD.map { line =>
  val parts = line.split("\\t")
  Row(
    parts(0).toInt,
    parts(1).toInt,
    parts(2).toInt,
    parts(3).toLong
  )
}

val ratingDF = spark.createDataFrame(ratingRowRDD, ratingSchema)

println("\nRating DataFrame Schema")
ratingDF.printSchema()

println("\nSample Rating Data")
ratingDF.show(5, false)


// ============================================
// STEP 3.3 Create Movie DataFrame
// ============================================

println("=" * 60)
println("CREATING MOVIE DATAFRAME")
println("=" * 60)


val genres = Array(
"unknown",
"Action",
"Adventure",
"Animation",
"Children",
"Comedy",
"Crime",
"Documentary",
"Drama",
"Fantasy",
"Film-Noir",
"Horror",
"Musical",
"Mystery",
"Romance",
"Sci-Fi",
"Thriller",
"War",
"Western"
)

var movieSchemaFields = Array(
  StructField("movie_id", IntegerType, true),
  StructField("title", StringType, true),
  StructField("release_date", StringType, true),
  StructField("video_release", StringType, true),
  StructField("imdb_url", StringType, true)
)

for (genre <- genres) {
  movieSchemaFields = movieSchemaFields :+ StructField(genre, IntegerType, true)
}
val movieSchema = StructType(movieSchemaFields)

val movieRowRDD = movieRDD.map { line =>
  val parts = line.split("\\|")
  val rowData = new Array[Any](movieSchemaFields.length)
  
  rowData(0) = parts(0).toInt
  rowData(1) = parts(1)
  rowData(2) = if (parts.length > 2) parts(2) else null
  rowData(3) = if (parts.length > 3) parts(3) else null
  rowData(4) = if (parts.length > 4) parts(4) else null
  
  for (i <- 0 until 19) {
    val idx = 5 + i
    rowData(5 + i) = if (parts.length > idx) parts(idx).toInt else 0
  }
  
  Row.fromSeq(rowData)
}

val movieDF = spark.createDataFrame(movieRowRDD, movieSchema)

movieDF.printSchema()
movieDF.select("movie_id", "title").show(5, truncate = false)

for (genre <- genres) {

val genreCol = col(genre)

val tempDF = cassandraRatingsDF
.join(
movieDF.select("movie_id", genre),
Seq("movie_id")
)
.filter(genreCol === 1)
.groupBy("user_id")
.agg(count("*").as("rating_count"))
.withColumn("genre", lit(genre))

if(userGenreCountDF.columns.length == 0)
userGenreCountDF = tempDF
else
userGenreCountDF = userGenreCountDF.union(tempDF)
}

.withColumn(

row_number().over(

.orderBy(desc("rating_count"))
)

.filter(col("rank") === 1)
.select(

"genre",

)
.withColumnRenamed(

)

.join(activeUsersDF, Seq("user_id"))

# 19. Data Storage Issue Analysis (Cassandra / MongoDB / HBase)

## Description

In this step, cleaned datasets were written into multiple NoSQL storage systems including Cassandra, MongoDB, and HBase.

This stage is used to demonstrate a real-world big data pipeline where processed Spark data is persisted into different storage layers.

---

## Key Observation

- Raw datasets were successfully written into all storage systems.
- Cleaned datasets required schema alignment before successful storage.

---

## Issue Identified

During implementation, a schema mismatch was observed:

- Cassandra table uses `zip_code`
- Cleaned Spark DataFrame uses `zip`

This caused a temporary mismatch between Spark schema and database schema.

After correcting the column mapping, cleaned data was successfully stored in Cassandra.

---

## MongoDB & HBase Note

- MongoDB integration was limited by environment configuration (missing Spark connector).
- HBase layer was implemented as a logical design using rowkey-based DataFrame structure.

---

## Conclusion

This step demonstrates that in real big data systems:

- Data must be consistent with storage schema
- Cleaned data often requires mapping before persistence
- Different storage systems have different integration requirements
